blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: State the reasons governments levy taxes, and keep direct and indirect taxation apart.

blocks.heading: What a tax is, and why it exists
blocks.text: A tax is a compulsory payment to a government, levied on income, spending or wealth, owed whether or not the payer receives any specific service in return. Taxes exist first to raise the revenue that pays for public spending: without them the budget would fund nothing. In Portugal a household meets them twice over - income tax on the payslip, value-added tax on the shopping bill - and both feed the same public accounts.

blocks.heading: Beyond revenue
blocks.text: Taxation also redistributes: a tax that takes a larger share of high incomes than of low ones transfers spending power towards poorer households, and the grants it funds do the same. And it corrects prices: a duty on tobacco makes the price carry more of the harm smoking imposes on others - the clinic time, the chest cases - steering buying away from a demerit good whose market price leaves that harm uncounted.

blocks.heading: Direct is not indirect
blocks.text: The confusion: learners treat every tax as one undifferentiated charge. The boundary: a direct tax is levied on income or profit and paid straight to the revenue authority by the person or firm taxed; an indirect tax is levied on spending and collected by the seller, who adds it to the price and passes it on. The test: ask what the charge falls on - income against spending - and who hands it over: the taxed party itself, or a trader collecting it from buyers.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Topic 4.1 set out why the state takes on these roles; topic 2.10 set out the harm a demerit good's price leaves uncounted.
